source_text: Προφανεῖς μὲν οὖν καὶ πᾶσαι αἱ ἄλλαι ἀρεταί, αἱ παρὰ τῷ Μωυσεῖ ἀναγεγραμμέναι, ἀρχὴν Ἕλλησι παντὸς τοῦ ἠθικοῦ τόπου παρασχόμεναι, ἀνδρείαν λέγω καὶ σωφροσύνην καὶ φρόνησιν καὶ δικαιοσύνην καρτερίαν τε καὶ ὑπομονὴν καὶ τὴν σεμνότητα καὶ ἐγκράτειαν τήν τε ἐπὶ τούτοις εὐσέβειαν. ἀλλ’ ἡ μὲν εὐσέβεια παντί που δήλη τὸ ἀνωτάτω καὶ πρεσβύτατον αἴτιον σέβειν καὶ τιμᾶν καὶ διδάσκουσα. καὶ δικαιοσύνην δὲ αὐτὸς ὁ νόμος παρίστησι παιδεύων τήν τε φρόνησιν διὰ τῆς τῶν αἰσθητῶν εἰδώλων ἀποχῆς καὶ τῆς πρὸς τὸν ποιητὴν καὶ πατέρα τῶν ὅλων προσκληρώσεως, ἀφ’ ἧς δόξης οἷον πηγῆς πᾶσα σύνεσις αὔξεται. θυσίαι γὰρ ἀνόμων βδέλυγμα κυρίῳ, εὐχαὶ δὲ κατευθυνόντων δεκταὶ παρ’ αὐτῷ. ἐπεὶ οιαῦτα καὶ τὰ παρὰ Ἡσαΐᾳ· τί μοι πλῆθος τῶν θυσιῶν ὑμῶν ὑμῶν; λέγει κύριος, καὶ πᾶσα ἡ περικοπή· λῦε πάντα σύνδεσμον ἀδικίας· αὕτη γὰρ θυσία θεῷ δεκτή, καρδία συντετριμμένη καὶ ζητοῦσα τὸν πεπλακότα. ζυγὰ δόλια βδέλυγμα ἔναντι θεοῦ, στάθμιον δὲ δίκαιον δεκτὸν αὐτῷ. ἐντεῦθεν ζυγὸν μὴ ὑπερβαίνειν Πυθαγόρας παραινεῖ. δικαιοσύνη δὲ δολία εἴρηται ἡ τῶν αἱρέσεων ἐπαγγελία, καὶ γλῶσσα μὲν ἀδίκων ἐξολεῖται, στόμα δὲ δικαίων ἀποστάζει σοφίαν. ἀλλὰ γὰρ τοὺς σοφοὺς καὶ φρονίμους φαύλους καλοῦσιν. μακρὸν δ’ ἂν εἴη περὶ τῶν ἀρετῶν τούτων μαρτυρίας παρατίθεσθαι, ἁπάσης ταύτας ἐξυμνούσης τῆς γραφῆς. ἐπεὶ δ’ οὖν τὴν μὲν ἀνδρείαν ὁρίζονται ἐπιστήμην δεινῶν καὶ οὐ δεινῶν καὶ τῶν μεταξύ, τὴν δὲ σωφροσύνην ἕξιν ἐν αἱρέσει καὶ φυγῇ σῴζουσαν τὰ τῆς φρονήσεως κρίματα, παράκειται τε τῇ μὲν ἀνδρείᾳ ἥ τε ὑπομονή, ἣν καρτερίαν καλοῦσιν, ἐπιστήμην ἐμμενετέων καὶ οὐκ ἐμμενετέων, ἥ τε μεγαλοψυχία, ἐπιστήμη τῶν συμβαινόντων ὑπεραίρουσα, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῇ σωφροσύνῃ ἡ εὐλάβεια, ἔκκλισις οὖσα σὺν λόγῳ. Φυλακὴ δὲ τῶν ἐντολῶν, τήρησις οὖσα αὐτῶν ἀβλαβής, περιποίησίς ἐστιν ἀσφαλείας βίου. καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ἄνευ ἀνδρείας καρτερικὸν εἶναι οὐδὲ μὴν ἄνευ σωφροσύνης ἐγκρατῆ. ἀντακολουθοῦσι δὲ ἀλλήλαις αἱ ἀρεταί, καἰ παρ’ ᾧ αἱ τῶν ἀρετῶν ἀκολουθίαι, παρὰ τούτῳ καὶ ἡ σωτηρία, τήρησις οὖσα τοῦ εὖ ἔχοντος. εἰκότως ἔτι περὶ τούτων διαλαβόντες τῶν ἀρετῶν περὶ πασῶν ἂν εἴημεν ἐσκεμμένοι, ὅτι ὁ μίαν ἔχων ἀρετὴν γνωστικῶς πάσας ἔχει διὰ τὴν ἀντακολουθίαν. αὐτίκα ἡ ἐγκράτεια διάθεσίς ἐστιν ἀνυπέρβατος τῶν κατὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον φανέντων. ἐγκρατεύεται δὲ ὁ κατέχων τὰς παρὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον ὁρμὰς ἢ ὁ κατέχων αὑτὸν ὥστε μὴ ὁρμᾶν παρὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον.
thought_title: Virtues in Greek and Christian Thought
pass_a_gloss: The other virtues, which are written by Moses, are evident and they provide a starting point for all ethical matters for the Greeks, I mean courage and self-control and prudence and justice and patience and perseverance and dignity and self-control and the piety that is based on these. But piety is evident to everyone as the highest and most ancient cause to reverence and honor and to teach. And the law itself presents justice, teaching prudence through the avoidance of sensible idols and the calling towards the creator and father of all, from which glory, as from a source, all understanding increases. For sacrifices of the lawless are an abomination to the Lord, but the prayers of the upright are acceptable to him. Since also the things from Isaiah say: what is the multitude of your sacrifices to me, says the Lord, and the whole passage: loose every bond of injustice, for this is a sacrifice acceptable to God, a heart that is broken and seeking the one who has been afflicted. False balances are an abomination before God, but a just scale is acceptable to him. From this, Pythagoras advises not to exceed the balance. But the justice of the heresies is said to be false, and the tongue of the unrighteous will be destroyed, but the mouth of the righteous will drip with wisdom. But they call the wise and prudent ones worthless. It would be long to present testimonies about these virtues, which all of scripture praises. Since, then, they define courage as the knowledge of what is fearful and not fearful and what is in between, and self-control as a habit that saves the judgments of prudence in choice and avoidance, perseverance, which they call patience, is placed beside courage, as the knowledge of what is to be endured and not to be endured, and magnanimity, as the knowledge of what happens that surpasses, but also caution is placed beside self-control, as a withdrawal with reason. The guarding of the commandments, being the blameless keeping of them, is the acquisition of the security of life. And it is not possible to be patient without courage or to be self-controlled without self-control. The virtues follow one another, and where there are the followings of the virtues, there is also salvation, being the keeping of what is good. It is reasonable, then, that having taken up these virtues, we would be concerned with all of them, because the one who has one virtue knowingly has all of them through their mutual following. Immediately, self-control is a disposition that is invincible regarding the things that appear according to the right reason. And one is self-controlled who holds back the impulses that are contrary to the right reason or who holds back oneself so as not to be impelled contrary to the right reason.

choices.why: The verb ἐγκρατεύεται is in the present tense, indicating a state of being.
The phrase ὀρθὸν λόγον refers to the correct or proper reason.
The noun ἀντακολουθίαν refers to the mutual or reciprocal following of the virtues.

bible_refs.note: The passage from Isaiah is quoted in the text.
The verse from Proverbs is referenced in the text.

pass_b_english: Clearly, the other virtues recorded by Moses—courage, self-control, prudence, justice, patience, perseverance, dignity, self-control, and the piety grounded in these—gave the Greeks a starting point for the whole field of ethics. Piety itself is evident to everyone as the highest and most ancient cause, teaching us to reverence, honor, and worship. The law itself presents justice, and it teaches prudence by turning us away from sensible idols and calling us toward the Creator and Father of all, from whose glory, as from a fountain, all understanding increases. For the sacrifices of the lawless are an abomination to the Lord, but the prayers of the upright are acceptable to him (Isaiah 1:11-17). So too the words in Isaiah: "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord," and the whole passage: "Loose every bond of injustice, for this is a sacrifice acceptable to God, a broken and contrite heart seeking the one who fashioned it" (Isaiah 1:11-17). False balances are an abomination before God, but a just scale is acceptable to him (Proverbs 11:1). From this, Pythagoras advises not to exceed the balance. But the justice of the heresies is called false, and the tongue of the unrighteous will be destroyed, but the mouth of the righteous drips with wisdom. Yet they call the wise and prudent worthless. It would take too long to set out testimonies about these virtues, since all of Scripture sings their praise. Since, then, they define courage as knowledge of what is fearful, what is not fearful, and what lies between, and self-control as a habit that preserves the judgments of prudence in choice and avoidance, perseverance—which they call patience—is joined to courage as knowledge of what must be endured and what must not, and magnanimity as knowledge that rises above what happens; and caution is joined to self-control as a reasoned withdrawal. Keeping the commandments, which is their blameless observance, is the acquisition of a secure life. And it is not possible to be patient without courage, nor to be self-controlled without self-control. The virtues follow one another, and where the sequence of the virtues is found, there also is salvation, which is the preservation of what is good. It is reasonable, then, that having taken up these virtues we should be versed in them all, because the one who possesses one virtue knowingly possesses them all through their mutual connection. In short, self-control is an invincible disposition toward the things that appear according to right reason. A person is self-controlled who restrains impulses contrary to right reason, or who restrains himself so as not to be driven contrary to right reason.
